units: pascals at the listener; times in seconds from the trigger break (shots, dry_fire) or from the start of the motion

maher_shaw_2010.source: R. C. Maher and S. R. Shaw, "Directional aspects of forensic gunshot recordings", AES 39th Int. Conf., 2010. Remington 870, 18 in barrel, Federal 2 3/4 in 00 buck. Microphones 3 m from the muzzle, gun and microphones 3 m above frozen grass so the ground reflection arrives about 10 ms late. Unweighted rms level of a 9 ms window (400 samples at 44.1 kHz from 50 samples before the blast): near 145 dB on axis, about 15 dB less behind the shooter, lowest value 129 dB (read from the text; the figure was not digitised)

murphy_tubbs_2007.source: W. J. Murphy and R. L. Tubbs, "Assessment of noise exposure for indoor and outdoor firing ranges", J. Occup. Environ. Hyg. 4:688-697, 2007 (NIOSH). Remington 870 12 gauge, 45.72 cm barrel, outdoor range. B&K 4136 microphone 1 m to the left of the shooter at the height of the shooter's ear. Peak levels of the weapons other than the two loudest, the 870 among them: 159.0 to 161.5 dB. One-third-octave spectra over 42.67 ms: the maximum falls between 500 and 800 Hz for most of the weapons. Reflections seen after the direct wave: tent and shooter at 3.58 and 4.23 ms, ground at 6.24 ms

kardous_willson_2004.source: C. A. Kardous and R. D. Willson, "Limitations of using dosimeters in impulse noise environments", J. Occup. Environ. Hyg. 1:456-462, 2004 (NIOSH). Remington 870 at an indoor range, B&K 4136 just outside the shooter's ear: peak 163 dB, impulse duration 456 microseconds

krammer.source: peak level at the shooter's ear for 12 gauge shotguns, 161.5 dB with an 18.5 in barrel and 151.5 dB with 28 in (W. Krammer, Ball State University, as reproduced in E.A.R. Inc.'s "Gunfire Noise Level Reference Chart"; a secondary source)

meinke_2017.source: D. K. Meinke et al., "Prevention of noise-induced hearing loss from recreational firearms", Semin. Hear. 38:267-281, 2017 (PMC5634813). Shotguns 152 to 170 dB peak at the left ear of a right-handed shooter; outdoor impulses typically shorter than 10 ms; spectral peaks between 400 and 2000 Hz

niosh_hhe_2013.source: NIOSH Health Hazard Evaluation Report 2013-0124-3208, Table B3: Remington 870 fired inside a shoothouse, microphones at instructor positions. Indoors, so it bounds the B-duration from above; it is not a target for an outdoor model

routh_maher_2016.source: T. Routh and R. C. Maher, "Determining the muzzle blast duration and acoustical energy of quasi-anechoic gunshot recordings", AES 141st Conv., 2016. Remington 870 with 3 in shells among ten firearms, 3 m, 500 kHz sampling: muzzle blast durations (93 % of energy) are of the order of 1 ms, longest for the shotgun, whose energy also accumulates most slowly. The values are in figures only, so this is used as a qualitative check

directivity_form.source: peak overpressure proportional to mu cos(theta) + sqrt(1 - mu^2 sin^2(theta)): the form of K. Fansler and E. Schmidt, "The prediction of gun muzzle blast properties utilizing scaling" (BRL, 1983) and Fansler, ARL-TR-1434 (1997). Recalled: DTIC refused automated requests, so the report was not re-read. mu is fitted here to the published shotgun levels, see calibration

blast_scaling.source: a release of energy E in air at pressure p0 has the scale radius R0 = (E / p0)^(1/3); weak-shock peak overpressure k p0 R0 / r and positive phase c_T R0 / c. E is the gas energy in the bore when the payload leaves, from the action simulation. k is fitted to the published levels (calibration); c_T is set so the buckshot load has the published 456 microsecond duration

friedlander.source: muzzle blast as a Friedlander wave, p = P (1 - t/T) exp(-t/T): R. P. Hamernik and K. D. Hsueh, "Impulse noise: some definitions, physical acoustics and other considerations", J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 90:189-196, 1991, as used by Routh and Maher (2016). Its negative phase is fixed by its form: -0.135 P at t = 2 T, zero net impulse

blowdown.source: quasi-steady isentropic emptying of the bore through the choked muzzle: p = p_e (1 + t/theta)^(-2 gamma/(gamma-1)), theta = 2/(gamma-1) * V/(A c0) * ((gamma+1)/2)^((gamma+1)/(2(gamma-1))); textbook gas dynamics (the gun-emptying problem of J. Corner, "Theory of the Interior Ballistics of Guns", 1950). Gas temperature from p V = m R T with the charge mass of the action simulation

jet_efficiency.source: acoustic efficiency of a supersonic exhaust jet, sound power / mechanical jet power, about 0.5 % (NASA SP-8072, "Acoustic loads generated by the propulsion system", 1971; recalled, not re-read)

jet_strouhal.source: jet mixing noise peaks near a Strouhal number of 0.2 on the fully expanded jet diameter and velocity (Lighthill; Tam, Annu. Rev. Fluid Mech. 27, 1995)

jet_source.source: the loudest part of a supersonic jet lies some diameters downstream of the nozzle, near the end of its core: 8 fully expanded diameters used. Behind the gun its noise therefore arrives later than the blast

jet_directivity.source: jet noise is strongest forward of the muzzle: +5 dB on the axis to -8 dB behind, relative to the mean over a sphere, as a + b cos(theta)

ground.source: grass: effective flow resistivity 150 to 300 kPa s/m^2 (T. F. W. Embleton, J. E. Piercy and G. A. Daigle, J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 74:1239-1244, 1983), 200 used, in the one-parameter impedance model of M. E. Delany and E. N. Bazley, Appl. Acoust. 3:105-116, 1970; plane-wave reflection coefficient at the angle of the reflected ray

stance.source: standing shooter, eye 1.62 m above the ground, bore level; the ear 0.10 m behind, 0.04 m beside and 0.01 m below the aiming eye (the same figures as the hk416 asset)

covered_line.source: a covered firing point on an outdoor range. A concrete pad, a plywood roof on rafters 2.7 m up, a painted block wall 3 m behind the shooter, open at the front and the sides, an earth backstop 50 m downrange. The layout is a choice, not a measurement of any range. Absorption coefficients are handbook values near 500 Hz to 1 kHz (concrete 0.02, plywood panel 0.10, painted block 0.05); the scattering coefficients, the half of the scattered sound taken to stay under the roof rather than leave through the open sides, and the berm (0.40, Lambert) are inferred. Murphy and Tubbs (2007) saw the same kind of early reflections under a fabric tent at an outdoor range

room.source: the default surroundings: an empty training room, 8.5 x 2.7 x 10 m: plywood-lined walls and ceiling on a concrete floor, the shooter 2 m from the back wall. The layout is a choice. Absorption: handbook values for a 3/8 in plywood panel (0.28, 0.22, 0.17, 0.09, 0.10, 0.11 from 125 Hz to 4 kHz) and smooth concrete, read at the three tail bands. Early reflections are image sources (J. B. Allen and D. A. Berkley, J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 65:943-950, 1979) out to 40 ms; after that a statistical tail with the Eyring decay time of each band (C. F. Eyring, 1930), whose energy rate is that of the image lattice for a source with the blast's directivity, 4 pi c <D^2> r_d^2 / (V D_d^2) per second relative to the direct wave: the method of the hk416 asset

outdoor_range.source: an outdoor range in a clearing in pine woods: grass, an earth backstop 50 m downrange (60 m wide, 6 m high, the berm of the covered firing point), woods from 15 m behind the backstop for 100 m (60 m to either side of the line of fire) and belts of woods 130 to 230 m to either side. The firing point is the covered one above; far listeners get its back wall (12 m wide) as one mirror reflection and nothing from its roof, whose reflections do not reach beyond its edge. The layout is a choice, not a survey of any range. Backstop: Lambert scattering, absorption 0.40 (inferred). Trees: single scattering by trunks as rigid cylinders, geometric acoustics, intensity I a sin(phi/2) / (2 R) at distance R from a trunk of radius a for scattering angle phi (P. M. Morse and K. U. Ingard, "Theoretical Acoustics", 1968, scattering from a cylinder, short-wave limit), weakened as (ka)^3 / (1 + (ka)^3) at long wavelengths, with extinction exp(-2 a n l) along l metres of woods. 500 stems per hectare of 0.12 m radius is a guess for a pine stand; branches, foliage and undergrowth scatter more and are left out, so the tree returns are a lower bound. Air: ISO 9613-1 at 25 C and 70 % humidity (chosen: a warm humid day). Ground at grazing angles: spherical-wave reflection coefficient Q = R + (1 - R) F(w) (C. F. Chien and W. W. Soroka, J. Sound Vib. 43:9-20, 1975) on Delany-Bazley grass. Distance: weak-shock decay and lengthening of a spherical wave, P = P1 / (r s), T = T1 s, s = sqrt(1 + k ln r), k = (gamma + 1) / (2 gamma) P1 / (p0 c T1), referred to 1 m (L. D. Landau, 1945; the form used by the hk416 asset). No path is shadowed by the backstop, and each return is single: no berm-to-trees or trees-to-ground paths

mechanical_scale.source: pascals at the shooter's ear per kg m/s of impact momentum, before the force spectrum and radiation weights. Set so that a brisk rack peaks near 105 dB at the ear. No published level for a pump action was found

hertz.source: contact time of an impact from Hertz's theory, t_c = 2.87 (m^2 / (R E*^2 v))^(1/5), with the moving mass from the model and the speed from the action simulation; contact radius 5 mm (guess). The force is a half sine of that length, so modes above about 1 / t_c are barely excited (K. L. Johnson, "Contact Mechanics", 1985)

structure.source: barrel, magazine tube: free-free bending of steel tubes of the model's size. Receiver walls: simply supported aluminium plates, 3 mm (notes/NOTES.md). Action bars: free-free steel strips 2.8 mm thick. Stock and forend shells: simply supported polymer plates 3 mm thick, E = 3 GPa, 1150 kg/m^3 (guess: a glass-filled polymer). Loss factors: steel tubes 0.008 to 0.01, receiver and bars 0.02, polymer 0.06 (inferred: a gun held in two hands). Radiation: (ka)^2 / (1 + (ka)^2) for plates, (ka)^3 / (1 + (ka)^3) for tubes in bending; a mode's share of the sound is the square root of that. How strongly each event drives each part is a guess (PART_WEIGHT, EVENTS)

hammer.source: hammer 30 g arriving at 4.5 m/s (about 0.3 J)

shooter.note: at the shooter's ear, behind the muzzle

bystander.note: 5 m to the side of the muzzle, at ear height

environments.range: the default: an outdoor range in a clearing in pine woods, the shooter under a covered firing point
environments.room: a plywood-lined training room, 8.5 x 2.7 x 10 m
environments.covered: the covered firing point and the backstop alone, without the woods
environments.free: free field, no reflection at all: the dry shot

rows.name: rms9 at 3 m, on axis (Maher and Shaw 2010)
rms9 at 3 m, behind (Maher and Shaw 2010)
peak 1 m left of the shooter (Murphy and Tubbs 2007, middle of 159.0 to 161.5)
peak at the shooter's ear (Krammer, 18.5 and 28 in interpolated to 20 in)

calibration.method: k (level) and mu (directivity) minimise the squared differences of these four levels, rendered in free field for the 00 buck load; c_T makes its positive phase the published 456 microseconds. Three numbers fitted to five published ones. The published guns have 18 and 18.5 in barrels, this one 20 in: the model has almost no barrel-length term, so the difference is ignored
